bollymeter.basis: 95% on Rotten Tomatoes from 195 critics. Colin Farrell's transformation and Cristin Milioti's scene-stealing Sofia Falcone gave critics what amounted to a character study wrapped in a mob drama - darker and more precise than superhero TV typically manages.

pull_quotes.text: A ferociously entertaining crime drama elevated by two powerhouse lead performances - and Colin Farrell is unrecognisable in the best possible way.

seasons.review_body: The Penguin is the best argument DC has made in years for the superhero-adjacent limited series format. Lauren LeFranc built eight episodes around Oz Cobb's ascent - and crucially, the show works as a crime drama first and a DC property second. Colin Farrell under three hours of prosthetics delivers a performance of genuine menace and dark comedy, but the critical surprise was Cristin Milioti as Sofia Falcone: wounded, brilliant, and terrifying. Critics pointed to the show's willingness to let Gotham be genuinely grimy - no CGI spectacle, mostly intimate rooms and bad decisions. The 5.3 million viewers at launch were the highest-rated HBO premiere in two years, and the critical score (95% RT) put it among the best DC productions ever made.

episode_reviews.title: After Hours
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Penguin picks up immediately after the Riddler's flooding of Gotham in The Batman (2022), dropping Oz Cobb into the power vacuum with nothing but audacity and tactical instinct. The premiere establishes the series' register - Sopranos-adjacent mob drama with superhero-adjacent origin story - and confirms that Colin Farrell's prosthetic transformation is matched by a performance of comparable depth.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Oz Cobb surveying a flooded, ruined Gotham and calculating exactly how to turn catastrophe into opportunity - the moment that defines the character for the entire run.
episode_reviews.review_body: The Penguin's premiere operates as a thesis statement: this is not a superhero series but a crime drama that happens to occupy a superhero-adjacent world. Set in the immediate aftermath of The Batman's Riddler flooding Gotham, the episode drops Oz Cobb into a power vacuum and watches him work. Colin Farrell's physical transformation via prosthetics is extraordinary, but the performance underneath it is the real achievement - Oz is calculating, resentful, and genuinely funny in ways that make him compelling even at his most brutal. At 95% on Rotten Tomatoes from 195 critics, the series earned that response largely from how the premiere established its tonal commitment. The decision to frame a Batman universe spinoff as a Sopranos-inflected character study proved immediately effective in the opening episode.

episode_reviews.title: Sofia in Wonderland
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Episode 3 is The Penguin's formal statement of ambition: a Sofia Falcone backstory episode that operates as a standalone psychological portrait. Cristin Milioti's performance is the episode's whole argument - what happens to a woman whose patrician family processes her as a liability. The episode reframes the entire season.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Sofia's account of Arkham - the specific, calm way she describes what happened to her there - the scene that makes the entire season's power dynamic suddenly legible.
episode_reviews.review_body:
# The Penguin S01E03: "Sofia in Wonderland" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

Election night opens with **Bella Reál** ahead of Acting Mayor **Tomlin**, the kind of Gotham news that should belong to podiums, crowds, and civic relief. The episode pushes that hope onto a roof, toward City Hall fireworks, then cuts the sky open with bombs. People drop. A name gets shouted into panic: **Calvin**. By the time **Oz** meets **Trey Bloom** and the new drug has a name, the hour has made its point. “Sofia in Wonderland” is about traps disguised as exits, and nobody walks through one without paying rent.

## Gotham Celebrates, Then Ducks

The opening stretch is the episode’s cleanest design choice, letting public life and street danger collide without speechifying. Reál leading Tomlin places Gotham in a fragile political moment. The roof plan to watch City Hall fireworks gives that moment a local, almost ordinary shape. Then the fatal skating story tied to Calvin, the shouted name, and the bombs turn civic spectacle into survival reflex.

That pivot matters. The hour runs on sudden changes in temperature: a scene moves through conversation, then danger snaps everyone downward. Gotham is a place where plans do not mature. They get interrupted.

The Calvin thread is the smartest seed in this opening because it arrives as a name, not an answer. Someone disappears around the same time another person did. That is enough to stain the scene. The episode does not solve the question here, and the restraint helps the season machinery. Calvin becomes a pressure point instead of a case file.

The opening strains under its own density. Political news, rooftop fireworks, Calvin, panic, and bomb imagery arrive fast. The compression gives the hour momentum, but it thins the emotional residue of the skating story. The show wants Calvin to haunt the episode. As plot pressure, he does. As feeling, the thread only gets halfway there.

## Bliss Is a Business Plan With Teeth

Once Oz is introduced to **Trey Bloom**, the episode shifts from Gotham panic to criminal product development. Trey cooks up the drug components, the drug is named Bliss, and the hour treats the name like a pitch deck with a pulse. Contraband becomes branding, distribution, price, and territory.

The best choice here is practical detail. By the time the party sales pitch begins, Bliss has a street shape: twenty a hit, sales reps moving product, and **Victor** forced into the most dangerous job for a person still pretending he has an exit. The line about bringing something new marks the commercialization point, but the setup does the harder work. The name lands earlier. The pitch lands later. The operation starts to look real before it starts to look safe.

Oz sharpens through this structure. He wants the trade to work under the new plan, while betrayal anxiety poisons every step. He knows his own moves could invite the same treatment back. The episode understands him as an operator who thrives on motion. Keep moving, and guilt has trouble catching up. Stop, and every deal has teeth.

Bliss gives Oz a future to sell while the episode keeps showing the cost of entering that future. The drug promises escape through sensation. The business around it removes escape from everyone handling it.

## Victor’s Exit Becomes His Assignment

Victor is the emotional hinge of the hour. His conflict is painfully direct: he wants out, specifically the California escape, but the episode pushes him into staying and acting as bagman for Bliss at the club. That turn works because Victor does not need to become a different person. He only needs to take one job he should refuse.

The bagman detail is crucial. The episode could have kept Victor near the operation as a nervous witness. Putting money and product movement in his hands makes his compromise physical. He is carrying the plan. That choice gives the episode its best moral sting. Victor’s dream of leaving does not vanish in a grand betrayal. It gets crowded out by logistics.

The club sales sequence gives this turn a nasty rhythm. The pitch begins, the price is set, the reps move, and Victor becomes the person through whom the plan circulates. For Oz, this is execution. For Victor, it is self-erasure by increments. The hour keeps him close enough to danger that escape starts to look childish, then cruelly proves why he wanted escape in the first place.

This is the episode’s strongest argument. Crime here is not glamorous seduction. It is scheduling. It is being told where to stand, what to carry, when to keep quiet. Victor’s tragedy is that he does not choose the whole life in one speech. He stays one more night.

## Sofia Asks for Trust in a Room Built to Deny It

**Sofia Falcone** gives the episode its title charge, even when the plot keeps shifting around Oz and Victor. Her goal is clear: she wants trust and business approval for Bliss. The obstacle is just as clear: **Feng Zhao** challenges her through her past and Arkham history. That confrontation gives the hour a harder edge because Sofia is selling herself as someone stable enough to build around.

Business approval here depends on confidence, and Sofia’s history becomes ammunition before the plan can stand on its own. The episode gets tension from that unfairness. Bliss may be the new thing in the room, but Sofia is the thing everyone thinks they already understand.

**Johnny Viti** adds another layer of rot. His coup-plan leverage and his willingness to call out Oz while backing restructuring and support claims make the room feel rigged from multiple angles. Nobody is evaluating Bliss in clean business terms. Everyone is counting advantage. Everyone is preparing a version of the story where they survive the next betrayal.

Zhao’s concern works better as pressure than as a fully textured counterargument. The episode needs him to doubt Sofia, and the doubt is useful. Still, the scene’s power comes less from Zhao himself than from what his objection does to Sofia: it forces her to argue for the future while being dragged back into the institutional shadow of Arkham.

## In It Now Means the Door Has Closed

The final interruption and attack complete the hour’s trap design. The episode begins with a public celebration becoming panic, then ends with the Bliss operation turning from plan into consequence. After the chaos, Victor and Oz declare they are in it now. The phrase lands because the hour has spent its runtime removing every soft exit.

For Oz, the closing beat tightens the betrayal question. His plan has advanced, but advancement does not mean control. It means exposure. He has a product, a network, pressure from power players, Sofia’s unstable path to approval, and Victor inside the machinery. Success and danger have become the same hallway.

For Victor, the line is harsher. His California escape was the clean version of his future. Acting as bagman was the compromise. The attack makes the compromise permanent, at least emotionally. Once violence seals the night, his presence in the operation cannot be treated as a temporary favor. First you help. Then you survive. Then someone tells you what that means.

The episode earns that ending, though its dialogue momentum occasionally squeezes the air out of individual beats. The long silences between transitions suggest the hour knows when to reset visually, but once conversations start, they keep pressing forward. That gives “Sofia in Wonderland” force. It also leaves a few emotional bruises underdeveloped.

## The Verdict

“Sofia in Wonderland” is a strong pressure-cooker episode that turns every promised escape into another form of commitment. The election-night bombs, the Calvin question, Bliss’s rollout, Sofia’s challenged authority, Johnny Viti’s leverage, and Victor’s bagman assignment all point in the same direction: Gotham does not let people leave cleanly. The craft is sharpest around Victor, whose California dream gets crushed one operational task at a time. The episode is less graceful when it stacks too many urgent beats close together, and Zhao’s challenge works better as pressure than as character. Still, the final “in it now” lands with bite. As a season piece, it pushes the Bliss operation from idea to consequence and leaves the next move looking dangerous from every angle.

verdict.one_liner: A tense, product-to-panic chapter where Bliss gives Oz momentum and turns Victor’s exit into a locked door.

episode_reviews.title: A Great or Little Thing
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Penguin's finale resolves the mob war it has been building since the premiere and delivers on Oz Cobb's coronation as the series' title character in both name and power. A satisfying close that earns its darkness without exploiting it, and leaves Gotham's gangland in a configuration the broader DC universe will have to reckon with.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Oz's final act against the Falcone family - the specific, precise nature of his vengeance, which makes his transformation into the Penguin feel inevitable rather than scripted.
episode_reviews.review_body: The finale of The Penguin delivers on the mob drama the series established in episode 1. Oz Cobb's arc from opportunistic lieutenant to crime lord completes itself here with a specificity the DC universe rarely achieves in its origin stories. The violence of the climax is earned rather than spectacular - the series has done the character work to make the Penguin's emergence feel inevitable. Sofia Falcone's arc reaches its conclusion in a way that maintains the co-protagonist structure that distinguished the series from a straightforward villain spinoff. At 95% RT and 8.2 IMDb, the finale contributes to a limited series that holds up as DC's best-executed character study in the streaming era.
